New document news. ParseBench hit 1.0. ParseBench is a document parser benchmark to test how well parsers work across text, formatting, tables, charts, and page locations. All of these matter when you need to point back to the source of a result and make sure that it is accurate.

The most important thing, however, is that 0.2 and earlier scores are not compatible with 1.0. If you use ParseBench and have old benchmarks, make sure to rerun them before running a new model on 1.0 and comparing. Rerun your old experiments on 1.0 and you will be good to go.

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
New document news. Nutrient released a new state model that predicts whether a field or checkbox is blank or filled.

Normally you would use a field detector, take each detected text box, checkbox, or signature, and send that small rectangle to the state model for the empty-versus-filled check. This is often very difficult, but very critical. For example, a signed legal document and an unsigned legal document should be treated very differently.

I ran it on a sample blank text field, which scored 0.007 filled. A typed text field scored 0.892 as filled. A checked box only scored 0.416. This one seemed pretty clear that it was checked, so it did not do quite as good a job there as I would like. The signature field with some lines in it scored essentially 1.0, which is what I would expect.

Overall, it seems pretty good. If I were to use this, I would probably do a little more checking around the checkboxes to see what needs to be done to handle that correctly and better. This is not a benchmark, but just a quick second-step check for me to do. If you use this in an application, I hope to hear how it works for you.

Source: https://huggingface.co/nutrientdocs/form-field-v1-state

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
NeoMME finds the right document page. I ran its released 260 million parameter checkpoint on three document pages.

It has two ways to search. The late-interaction mode breaks up a page into many vectors. The lighter, dense mode reduces it to one vector per page.

First, I searched insurance documents for a health insurance claim form, and both modes returned the correct page. I then searched a document for a restaurant food inspection report, and again both modes returned the correct page.

Then I searched a trickier two-page procurement form where the form spans both pages, but I was looking for the start of the form. The late-interaction mode returned the first page just like I wanted. The lighter, dense mode put the second page first. It did not work quite as well, but it was not a complete failure. This is page two of the form instead of page one.

It was pretty cool to see the late-interaction mode get all three of these checks right. The lighter mode got one wrong, but it was a reasonable failure. This is a small test, but it is just enough to show that it does seem to work as expected. I hope you check it out and try it on larger systems.

Source: https://x.com/tonywu_71/status/2095501116033126584

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
New document news. LlamaIndex added a Turbo mode in beta for much lower latency. This is super important when you have something users wait on, like uploading a document to answer questions, do retrieval, or create a report.

I compared Turbo and Cost Effective mode on the same examples from my document lab. On a JPMorgan balance sheet, Turbo finished in 10.5 seconds, where Cost Effective took 41.2 seconds, about 4 times faster. On a Vanguard table, Turbo took 9 seconds instead of 30 seconds, about 3.3 times faster. Both returned identical correct values on both documents, so there was no accuracy trade-off on either of them.

Turbo is 35 credits per page, where Cost Effective is 8 credits per page. Turbo is fast, expensive, and great for regular documents. Cost Effective is slow, cheap, and great for regular documents. Agentic and Agentic Plus are slow, expensive, but very accurate on really hard documents.

Overall, Turbo seems like a great fit when you need fast extraction while users are waiting. In these tiny experiments, Turbo delivered the claimed speed without the extraction quality trade-off. It wasn't a full independent benchmark, just a few tests.

More Document News: https://isaacflath.com/news

New Document News. LlamaIndex and Kaggle just released ExtractBench, which is a benchmark for getting structured data out of enterprise-type documents. It has about 5,000 pages in it, 370 documents, and it's across eight different domains and lots of different categories.

The input is a full document with a user-defined JSON schema. Then the output is all of the values that it should extract. For the extracted values, it also asks for a page number or a bounding box, so you have citations with that.

Looking through it, there are long tables, cross-page continuations, forms with checkboxes, W-2s, presentations, dense tables, electric bills, and signatures.

This seems like a really practical dataset. I think it's brand new, so I wouldn't necessarily trust the leaderboard yet, but hopefully in a week or two everyone will be testing their models against it and we can see where it shakes out.

OCR on signatures is difficult and critical on documents to know if they can be used (like legal or medical documents).

In this case Gemini marked all four signatures as signed. AWS Textract found 3 out of 4 signature regions, with confidence scores from 32% to 41%.

The page has two really clear signatures and two with faint marks.  Maybe from repeated scans before the final signature, or maybe an erased signature.

It's important to include non-perfect and faded signatures in your eval set and decide how to handle them.

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
Speculative decoding can cut LLM latency in half even though it does more total work.

At low batch sizes, generating one token spends most of its time loading model weights from memory while the GPU’s compute units sit idle. Verifying several drafted tokens uses that idle compute, so the extra work is nearly free.

At high batch sizes, the GPU is already busy and the speedup disappears. You  can turn speculation off automatically when batches get large.

Comment “SpecDecode” for the full post.

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
Most ways to make an LLM faster trade away some quality. Diffusion models can lose accuracy, and quantization can reduce quality as it compresses the weights.

Speculative decoding decreases latency without a quality penalty. A small model drafts tokens, but the large model verifies every one. The final output is mathematically guaranteed to come from the same distribution as the large model running alone.

Comment “SpecDecode” for the full post.

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
One OCR bounding box can take 13 tokens. With normal LLM decoding, that means 13 forward passes.

Speculative decoding lets a small model guess several tokens ahead. The larger model checks them in one pass, keeps the correct prefix, and replaces the first wrong token. 

Comment “SpecDecode” for the full post.

posts.author_bio: Teaching builders how to extract and use information from documents to make better, faster decisions
posts.post_caption:
The LLM OCRs twice as fast with the same output quality because of speculative decoding.

Normally, an LLM predicts one token at a time. With speculative decoding small fine tuned draft model predicts several tokens ahead, then the larger model verifies those guesses in parallel.

Half the latency with no quality hit.

Comment “SpecDecode” for the full post
